newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian president faces more challengers.
newsitem.headline: Estonian president faces more challengers.

text.p: Two more candidates stepped forward on Tuesday to challenge Estonian President Lennart Meri as he renews his bid for a second term in office.
A 374-strong electoral college will vote on Meri's re-election on September 20 after it was rejected three times by the Baltic state's parliament last month.
The refusal to back Meri was seen as a rebuke for over-stepping the bounds of what is largely a ceremonial role.
Right-wing politician Tunne Kelam, rated as a strong candidate, and the deputy leader of the leftist Centre Party, Sirri Oviir, said they would stand against Meri.
Meri's arch-rival Arnold Ruutel, a former Communist and a leader of Estonia's drive to regain its independence in 1991, was the only other confirmed candidate.
Kelam, like Ruutel a parliament deputy speaker, said he wanted to dispel the myth that Meri was the only choice.
"In a democracy you have choice," Kelam told a news conference. "Phrases like 'the only one' and 'irreplaceable' are bad for democracy."

The winning candidate needs the support of more than half of the electoral college and Kelam is expected to take votes from Meri. Commentators say Kelam's standing increases the chance the electoral college vote will be inconclusive.
Meri and Ruutel battled through the three rounds of parliamentary voting in which Meri led but never came close to getting the 68 votes he needed in the 101-seat house.
Highly rated for his charm and charisma on the international stage, Meri has been accused at home of assuming too much power.

The strongest criticism levelled against him is that he signed a deal in 1994 on the withdrawal of Russian troops without consulting parliament and which left too many former Soviet military pensioners in Estonia.
There will be two rounds of voting by the electoral college. If both are inconclusive, parliament will vote again.
